findings.summary: `java-test-fixtures` is applied with a comment citing testing.md rule 19 -- 'a home shared by T1 and T3 rather than a copy each' -- but neither half of that property holds. Verified by construction against the staged tree: (a) `src/testFixtures` has neither JUnit nor AssertJ on its compile classpath (`testFixturesImplementation` is created by the plugin and populated by nothing; the `testing { suites { withType<JvmTestSuite> } }` block at :64-70 reaches only test suites, not the fixtures source set), so an abstract `@Test`-bearing conformance base class fails with 'package org.junit.jupiter.api does not exist'; (b) the registered suites at :91-96 declare `implementation(project())` only, never `testFixtures(project())`, so a plain fixture class is 'cannot find symbol' from BOTH `compileIntegrationTestJava` and `compileClusterTestJava`. Only the built-in `test` suite sees fixtures, and even it cannot see a fixture that imports JUnit. The comment asserts a property that is empirically false, which is the 'gate that reports success while checking nothing' class applied to test infrastructure. Confirmed fixable in-scaffold: adding `testFixturesImplementation` for junit-bom/junit-jupiter/assertj-core plus `implementation(testFixtures(project()))` in both registered suites makes an abstract Conformance base class in `src/testFixtures` compile and its T1 and T3 subclasses both run (`:format:integrationTest` executed, BUILD SUCCESSFUL).
findings.failure_scenario: At M0.18 the store conformance suite (testing.md rule 19, the highest-weight suite in the standard) cannot be written where this commit says it goes. The author hits 'package org.junit.jupiter.api does not exist' in src/testFixtures and 'cannot find symbol' from integrationTest, and takes the cheapest exit: copy the suite into src/test and src/integrationTest, which is exactly the per-tier copy rule 19 forbids. The two copies then drift, and the CAS-rejection probe that rule 19 requires ('establish Capabilities by writing and asserting rejection, never from a version string') gets asserted against MemoryBinStore in the T1 copy and quietly dropped from the MinIO copy -- so a provider whose conditional write does not reject is never caught, and the silent divergence that breaks ordering ships green. The alternative exit is worse: drop T3 conformance entirely, leaving every backend claim resting on the in-memory fake.

findings.summary: The licence gate is genuine -- all six claimed failures were constructed and each fails with its own specific message and no other (missing sha, sha mismatch, unused sha, missing LICENSE, denied SPDX id, missing SPDX entry), plus absent `licenses/` and absent `SPDX.txt`; it is wired into both `check` and `build`, and `outputs.upToDateWhen { false }` was confirmed to keep it failing on a second consecutive run rather than going UP-TO-DATE. Transitive coverage is real (4 catalogue aliases resolve to 10 pinned jars). The non-cacheability trade is sound: re-measured, the whole `dependencyLicenses` invocation is ~450-650 ms wall clock, consistent with the recorded 567/543 ms, i.e. the cost is Gradle startup and the gate itself is free. The remaining hole is that the checked set is the root `licenseCheck` configuration built from the version catalogue, not the modules' actual resolved graphs. The diff discloses this at :27-30 and points at M0.19, so this is a note on a known limitation rather than a hidden defect.
findings.failure_scenario: A module's build.gradle.kts declares a literal coordinate (or a `compileOnly` OpenSearch SPI jar, or a `platform()`) instead of a catalogue alias. That artifact never enters `licenseCheck`, so it acquires no sha pin and no licence file, and `dependencyLicenses` still reports BUILD SUCCESSFUL with a stamp reading 'ok 10 jar(s)'. A GPL-2.0-only dependency added that way passes `check` today, and the deny-list -- which was verified to work correctly on everything it is given -- never sees it. Until M0.19 makes membership a predicate, the completeness claim is enforced by habit, and the green gate reads identically in both cases.
